points.label: Learning from labeled examples
points.description: The learner states that supervised learning trains a model on examples where the correct answer (label) is provided, so the model learns by comparing its predictions to the known answers.

points.label: Goal is generalization to new inputs
points.description: The learner explains that the point of supervised learning is not to reproduce the training answers but to generalize: to predict correct labels for new, unseen inputs.

points.label: Classification vs regression
points.description: The learner distinguishes the two main supervised task types: classification predicts a discrete category (e.g. spam/not-spam) and regression predicts a continuous number (e.g. a price), giving a correct example of at least one.

misconceptions.summary: In supervised learning a human supervises the model live, correcting each prediction by hand as it trains.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that 'supervision' refers to the labels in the dataset acting as the answer key; the comparison and correction loop is automatic during training, with no human intervening on individual predictions.

misconceptions.summary: If a model scores perfectly on its training examples, the learning has fully succeeded.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that success is measured on held-out unseen data, because perfect training performance can come from memorization; a model that fails on new inputs has not learned in the useful sense.

beginner: Where do the 'right answers' come from in the first place? Does someone have to write them all down?
Is predicting tomorrow's temperature supervised learning? What would the labels be there?
confident: Supervised learning means an engineer watches the model train and manually fixes its mistakes one by one.
Classification and regression are just two names for the same thing since both predict something.
skeptic: Labeling millions of examples costs a fortune and labelers disagree with each other. Doesn't supervised learning just launder human inconsistency into a model?
If the model only ever imitates the labels we gave it, can it ever do better than the humans who labeled the data?
